teaser: A green face, a red hat, and a nickname earned with a cup of hot chocolate.
review_notes:
Warhol comparison (turquoise and colored Marilyns, 1960s) is an editorial parallel, not a documented influence.
Nickname story (model asked for hot chocolate, 'Schokolade') is the traditional account.
Support stated as oil on cardboard: confirm with Columbus Museum of Art.
A related painting, Schokko with Wide-Brimmed Hat, sold at Sotheby's in 2008 for more than 18 million dollars: verify figure.
Jawlensky had 72 works confiscated from German museums in 1937: commonly cited number.
Image shows the Columbus version (red hat, fan), consistent with the listed work.

lesson.text: In the 1960s Andy Warhol printed Marilyn Monroe with a turquoise face, a pink face, an orange face. People called it Pop. Yet a Russian painter in Munich had already given a young woman a mint green face under a blazing red hat in 1909. Her skin was never meant to look like skin.

The painter was Alexej von Jawlensky, a former officer of the Russian army who had quit the military to paint. He had lived in Munich since 1896. In Paris he had seen the canvases of Matisse and his friends, nicknamed the “wild beasts” for their raw color, and he came home convinced that color could do the talking on its own.

Nobody is sure of the sitter's real name. She was a girl from a village near Munich who posed in Jawlensky's cold studio and, the story goes, kept asking for a cup of hot chocolate, “Schokolade” in German. The household nicknamed her Schokko, and the name stuck to the paintings.
So why green? Nobody in 1909 would have mistaken it for a likeness, and Jawlensky did not intend one. The answer is in how the face is built, piece by piece, from only four or five colors.

lesson.title: A face in four colors
lesson.text: Follow how Jawlensky constructs a head without any flesh tone.

spots.title: Green for light
spots.text: The lit side of the face is pale mint, the shadow along the cheek a deeper green. Light and shade are both there, simply translated into another color.

spots.title: Eyes like stained glass
spots.text: Thick black lines ring the eyes and draw the brows and nose. They lock each color in place, the way lead strips hold the panes of a church window.

spots.title: The mouth
spots.text: A small, closed pink mouth, set slightly off to the side. It is the warmest spot in the face and the only hint of her mood: reserved, a little bored.

spots.title: The scarf
spots.text: A knot of red-orange under the chin repeats the hat. The cool face is caught between two fires.

lesson.text: Green and red sit opposite each other on the color wheel. Painters call such pairs complementary colors: placed side by side, each makes the other look stronger. Here the red hat looks hotter because of the green face, and the face looks cooler because of the hat. Realistic skin would have dulled both.
Jawlensky also ties the two halves together with small echoes, so the picture does not split into a hot zone and a cold zone. One of them is easy to miss.
A drop of the face's cool turquoise has landed in the middle of the hot red hat. Where is it?

spots.title: The turquoise button
spots.text: A blue-green dot sits in the hollow of the hat brim, ringed with olive. It carries the color of the face and the background up into the red, like a rhyme.

lesson.text: The same trick runs the other way at the bottom, where a blue fan is sprinkled with red, yellow and orange dabs. In the summer of 1908 Jawlensky had painted in the market town of Murnau with Wassily Kandinsky, Gabriele Münter and Marianne von Werefkin. All four came back using flat, bright areas and dark contours like these.

The picture is painted on cardboard, not canvas. Jawlensky liked this cheap, stiff support for many works of these years: the board soaks up some of the oil and leaves the paint with a dry, matte glow.
Color in a portrait does not have to describe. Here it expresses: a green face is not a sick face, it is the temperature of the whole picture.

Jawlensky spent the rest of his life painting faces, each one simpler than the last, until they were only a few bars for eyes, nose and mouth. In 1937 the Nazi regime removed 72 of his works from German museums as “degenerate.” In 2008 another portrait of the same chocolate-loving girl sold at auction for more than 18 million dollars.

quiz.question: Where does the name “Schokko” come from?
options: It was the model's family name
The model kept asking for hot chocolate
It is the Russian word for hat
quiz.explanation: The nickname comes from “Schokolade,” the hot chocolate she asked for in the studio.

quiz.question: Why does the red hat look so intense?
options: It sits next to its complementary color, green
It is covered in gold leaf
quiz.explanation: Red and green are complementary, so each strengthens the other.

quiz.question: What do the thick black outlines do?
options: Show the sitter is in mourning
Lock each area of color in place, like lead in stained glass
quiz.explanation: The contours separate and hold the flat color areas.

quiz.question: What is the painting made on?
quiz.explanation: Jawlensky painted it in oil on cardboard, which gives a matte surface.

quiz.question: What did Jawlensky do before becoming a painter?
options: He was an officer in the Russian army
quiz.explanation: He left the Russian military to devote himself to painting.

facts.text: The green face means the sitter was ill.
facts.explanation: Green stands for light and shade and plays against the red; it is not a symptom.

facts.text: A turquoise dot in the hat repeats the color of the face.
facts.explanation: The small button in the brim echoes the cool tones below.

facts.text: In 1937 Jawlensky was celebrated by the Nazi regime.
facts.explanation: On the contrary, 72 of his works were removed from German museums as “degenerate.”
